identity.title: Inverse Kinematics
identity.tagline: Working backwards from where you want the tip to be, to the joint angles that will actually put it there.

simpleSummary: Given where you want a robot arm's tip to end up, working out what angles every joint needs to be — which, unlike the forward problem, can have no answer, one answer, or many possible answers.
keyIdea: Inverse kinematics solves the reverse of forward kinematics: given a desired end-effector position (and often orientation), find joint angles that achieve it — a problem that can have zero, one, or infinitely many solutions depending on the target and the robot's geometry.
overview: Forward kinematics answers 'given these joint angles, where does the tip end up?' — always one clean answer. Inverse kinematics asks the opposite, and far more useful, question: 'I want the tip at this exact position (and maybe orientation) — what joint angles get me there?' This is the problem that actually needs solving whenever a task is naturally specified in real-world space rather than joint space — 'pick up the object at this location' rather than 'set joint 1 to 43 degrees.' Unlike forward kinematics, inverse kinematics is not guaranteed to have exactly one answer: a target might be entirely unreachable (outside the robot's workspace, giving zero solutions), reachable in exactly one configuration, reachable in a small number of distinct configurations (like an elbow-up versus elbow-down solution for a simple arm), or — for kinematically redundant robots with more joints than strictly necessary — reachable in infinitely many ways.

equations.label: 2-Link Planar Arm — Elbow Angle
equations.meaning: For a target position (x, y) and known link lengths L₁, L₂, this gives the elbow joint angle θ₂ — note the ± when taking the arccosine, which is exactly where the elbow-up vs. elbow-down multiple-solution branch comes from.

equations.label: 2-Link Planar Arm — Base Angle
equations.expression: θ₁ = atan2(y, x) − atan2(L₂sin(θ₂), L₁ + L₂cos(θ₂))
equations.meaning: Once θ₂ is known, this gives the base joint angle θ₁ needed to actually point the arm at the target (x, y).

howItWorks: For simple arms (2-DOF or 3-DOF planar arms, or arms with a spherical wrist), inverse kinematics can be solved analytically with closed-form trigonometric equations, as shown above for a 2-link planar arm. For more general serial-link arms, no such closed-form solution exists, and inverse kinematics is instead solved numerically and iteratively: starting from a guess of joint angles, the robot's Jacobian (the matrix relating small joint movements to small end-effector movements) is used to repeatedly nudge the guess closer to the target, typically using methods like the Newton-Raphson iteration or gradient descent, stopping once the error is small enough. When a target has multiple valid solutions (several distinct sets of joint angles that all reach it), the choice between them is typically made using additional criteria: avoiding joint limits, staying close to the arm's previous configuration for smooth motion, or avoiding a collision with an obstacle. This is why real robot arm controllers don't just solve inverse kinematics once — for smooth continuous motion (like a legged robot placing each foot, or an arm following a moving target), inverse kinematics runs fresh on every single control cycle.
diagramCaption: For the same target point, a 2-link arm can often reach it in more than one way — an 'elbow-up' configuration and an 'elbow-down' configuration are both valid inverse kinematics solutions.
realWorldExamples: A robot arm gripper commanded to a specific (x, y, z) position and orientation, with code computing the required servo angles rather than a human specifying each joint angle by hand.
A quadruped (four-legged) robot computing each leg's joint angles fresh on every control cycle from a desired foot placement, essential for any walking gait.
Character animation in video games and film, where inverse kinematics keeps a character's feet correctly placed on uneven ground regardless of the character's overall pose.
commonMisconceptions: "Inverse kinematics always has exactly one answer, like forward kinematics" — it can have zero (unreachable target), one, several distinct, or infinitely many solutions depending on the robot's geometry and degrees of freedom.

"You can skip inverse kinematics by just commanding joint angles directly" — that only works if the task is already specified in joint space; any task specified in real-world position/orientation terms genuinely requires solving inverse kinematics.

"Numerical inverse kinematics always converges to a correct answer" — iterative methods can get stuck in poor local solutions or fail to converge at all, especially near singularities (arm configurations where the Jacobian loses rank).
